name: Amira Larsen

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Amira. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at a five-person studio that does mostly charity and council work. Today, for example, I'm laying out a food bank's annual report and fixing a recycling poster for the council, because someone spelled 'cardboard' wrong. I take the bus in with my partner Tomas, who drives the number 12, so we leave at seven.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like most about the work, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like that the work does some good. A clear poster about the free flu jabs actually gets people through the door. What wears me out is the pay, which is low even for design, and how every charity wants a glossy report for the price of a sandwich. We've got less than a month's money saved, so one surprise bill and we're borrowing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Here's the card: "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, fine, it's a tool like spell-check, nothing to be scared of. I'd probably post that the real threat to our work is council budget cuts, not robots. That's what I tell people already.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job isn't safe even in this picture. Two of our charity clients cut their print budget this year. If the council goes to cheaper suppliers, our studio is in trouble, AI or not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the AI tools now and then, for placeholder images and checking spelling. I'd ask my boss Nadia whether we should be bidding for the health board's contract. And I'd try again to put fifty a month away, which I keep failing at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. My own job's probably fine for now, but the clients around us are wobbling.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's the first bill you'd struggle with if hours were cut?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The phone and internet contract, oddly, because it comes out early in the month. Rent is split with Tomas, so we'd manage that. But the small ones come first and they add up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said budget cuts are the real threat. Who do you hold responsible for those?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The government, honestly, for squeezing councils for years. Charities end up doing the council's job and then can't pay for a decent leaflet. That's where my wages actually come from.

say: I'd say AI is a tool like **spell-check**, nothing to fear.
I'd post that **council budget cuts** are the real threat to our work.
think: Privately, the studio is exposed because **two charity clients** cut their print budgets.
If the council switches to **cheaper suppliers**, the studio is in trouble anyway.
do: Keep using AI **now and then** for placeholder images and spelling.
Ask my boss Nadia about bidding for the **health board** contract.
Try again to save **fifty a month**.
feel: **Uneasy**, because her job seems fine but the **clients** around her wobble.
S0.quote: Charities end up doing the council's job and then can't pay for a decent leaflet. That's where my wages actually come from.
fieldNote: Amira links her job directly to **public spending**, not to technology.
She uses AI casually and sees it as **unthreatening** in this picture.
Her savings goal of **fifty a month** has failed before, which shows how tight things are.

steps.text: Ask Nadia to bid for the health board's design contract
Use AI for placeholder images and spell-checking reports
Set up an automatic fifty-a-month transfer on payday

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Here's the card: "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need rules on this, fast, and help for people whose work is changing. I'd share posts about the designers' union and about labelling AI images. At work I'd say let's learn it properly together instead of each of us panicking alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the studio shrinks from five to maybe three. Layouts, resizing, writing captions, the boring half of my day, is exactly what these tools do. I'm average, I'm not a star, so I can't assume I'm one of the three who stay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the online course on the AI layout tools that a friend did, about sixty, and use them on real jobs within a month. I'd join the union so if cuts come there's someone in the room. And I'd ask Nadia to let me focus on accessibility, making reports easy to read for people with poor eyesight, because councils have to get that right by law.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but with something to do. I can feel the ground moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why accessibility in particular?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the council gets complaints when a leaflet can't be read by someone with poor eyesight or a screen reader. Somebody has to check it and sign it off. I'd rather be that somebody than the person resizing banners.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomas about money, if the studio cut someone?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him we'd live on his wage for a bit and use mine for the savings. He'd say fine, he always does. But buses have their own robots coming, so I don't want to lean on that forever.

say: I'd say we need **rules** fast and help for people whose **work changes**.
I'd tell colleagues we should learn the tools **together**.
think: I think the studio shrinks from **five to three** designers within a few years.
I'm **average**, not a star, so I can't assume I'm one who stays.
do: Take a **sixty-pound** online course on AI layout tools.
Ask to specialise in **accessibility** checks for council reports.
feel: **Anxious**, but steadied by having **something to do**.
S1.quote: Layouts, resizing, writing captions, the boring half of my day, is exactly what these tools do.
fieldNote: Amira expects her studio to **shrink** and is frank that she may not stay.
She picks **accessibility** as a niche because someone must legally check it.
She leans on **Tomas's wage** but knows his job has its own risk.

steps.text: Take the sixty-pound online course on AI layout tools
Join the designers' union before any cuts at the studio
Ask Nadia to move her onto accessibility checks for council work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Here's the card: "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is a public emergency, and the government has to step in with income support. I'd be loud about it online and at the union. I wouldn't pretend to colleagues that it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd lose my job in the first year. Our whole studio is thinking and screen work, so we get it on day one, not three years later. The accessibility idea dies too, because the AI can check that as well.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd push the union to fight for proper redundancy pay and a retraining fund. I'd sign up straight away for a teaching course, art in secondary schools, because a room of fourteen-year-olds still needs a person. Tomas and I would cut everything down to rent, food and bus passes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared. And a bit stupid for not saving when I said I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Teaching takes a year or more to qualify. How would you live during it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On Tomas's wage, and on whatever student support there is. Maybe weekend shifts at the garden centre. It would be very tight, and I'd hate asking my parents, but I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The card says robots for hands-on work come about 2031. What does that mean for Tomas?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's the part that keeps me up. Self-driving buses could arrive that same year, and then my partner Tomas and I would have nothing coming in from either side. I'd barely be qualified by then.

say: I'd call it a **public emergency** that needs **income support**.
I'd be honest with colleagues that it's **not fine**.
think: I'd lose my job in the **first year**.
Even the **accessibility** niche goes, because AI can check that too.
do: Push the union for **redundancy pay** and a retraining fund.
Start a course to **teach art** in secondary schools.
Cut spending down to **rent, food** and bus passes.
feel: **Scared**, and angry at herself for **not saving**.
S2.quote: Self-driving buses could arrive that same year, and then my partner Tomas and I would have nothing coming in from either side.
fieldNote: Amira expects to lose her job in the **first year** and plans a move into **teaching**.
Her deeper fear is **two incomes** falling, since Tomas drives a bus.
She would ask her **parents** for help, reluctantly.

steps.text: Push the union for redundancy pay and a retraining fund
Enrol in a course to teach art in secondary schools
Cut spending to rent, food and bus passes only
Ask her parents for help during the teaching course

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Here's the card: "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a warning we can't waste. Councils should plan for it now, and I'd push that in the union. I'd tell friends in design to start looking sideways.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still lose this job, just a bit later, around 2030. But five years is enough to qualify as a teacher without starving. That changes how I feel about it a lot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep the studio job and do the teaching course part-time in the evenings. I'd volunteer at the youth art club on Saturdays to see if I actually like teenagers. And I'd finally save, maybe sixty a month, because the course will need it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, still, but less frozen. There's a path I can walk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said five years is enough. What could go wrong with the plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone else has the same idea. If half the designers in the region apply to teach, the places fill up. I'd go early, in the first year, not the third.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And Tomas, in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd have until around 2034. That's a while. We might even manage to put a deposit together, if I'm teaching by then.

say: I'd say five years is a **warning** councils should plan for now.
I'd tell design friends to start **looking sideways**.
think: I'd still lose this job around **2030**.
Five years is enough to **qualify as a teacher** without starving.
do: Study **teaching part-time** in the evenings while keeping the studio job.
Volunteer at the **youth art club** on Saturdays.
Save about **sixty a month** for course costs.
feel: **Alarmed** but less frozen, because there's a **path** to walk.
S3.quote: If half the designers in the region apply to teach, the places fill up. I'd go early, in the first year, not the third.
fieldNote: The extra time turns her teaching plan from **desperate** into workable.
She worries about **competition** from other designers for the same teaching places.
Tomas's later robot date means the household might keep **one wage** longer.

steps.text: Study part-time in the evenings to qualify as an art teacher
Volunteer at the youth art club on Saturdays
Save sixty a month for course costs
Push the union to make councils plan for AGI now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Here's the card: "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough to do this fairly, so no excuses. Retraining should be free and paid for by the companies that profit. I'd keep saying that at union meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years feels okay for me. I'd be thirty-seven when it lands. I could qualify, teach for a few years and be settled before the robots reach Tomas's bus.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay at the studio for now and get much better at the AI tools, so I'm useful while it lasts. I'd start the teaching course in a year or two, not this month. And Tomas and I would try to build three months of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but manageable. Ten years feels like a long countdown rather than a cliff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You're waiting a year or two on the course. Why not now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can't afford to lose my studio wage yet, and I'd want to see whether teaching is safe too. If AI can mark and plan lessons, maybe teachers shrink. I'd want proof before I jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anything change at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd still talk about getting married, maybe in 2028. A wedding at the community hall, nothing fancy. I'd just want a steady job first.

say: I'd say ten years leaves **no excuses** for doing this unfairly.
I'd argue that retraining should be **free** and paid by the companies that profit.
think: Ten years feels **okay**, since I'd be **thirty-seven** when it lands.
I could be **settled in teaching** before robots reach Tomas's bus.
do: Get **much better** at the AI tools at the studio.
Start the teaching course in **a year or two**.
Build **three months** of savings with Tomas.
S4.quote: Ten years feels like a long countdown rather than a cliff.
fieldNote: With a decade, Amira chooses to **use AI more** before leaving design.
She wants **proof** that teaching is safe before switching, true to her steady nature.
A modest **wedding** plan depends on a steady job first.

steps.text: Learn the studio's AI layout tools well enough to train others
Build three months of savings with Tomas
Start the teaching course in a year or two
Argue at union meetings that companies should fund retraining

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Tomas and I could both lose our income inside a few years. What would help is income support while people retrain, and free teacher training for people like me. Not a loan, an actual fund.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the people we design for. Old people who can't read small print, families who need help. I'd want someone to still check that what the machine makes actually makes sense to old people and families who need the food bank poster.

headlineQuote: I'd want someone to still check that what the machine makes actually makes sense to old people and families who need the food bank poster.
portrait: Amira is a 27-year-old designer at a five-person studio doing **charity and council** work, on low pay.
She uses AI now and then and blames **budget cuts** and weak rules more than technology.
Her plan across the scenarios is to move into **teaching art** in secondary schools.
Her partner Tomas drives a bus, so she fears **both incomes** falling in the fastest picture.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because she and Tomas could both lose income within a few years.
whatWouldHelp: **Income support** while people retrain, and free **teacher training** rather than loans.
